title: Wimbledon 2026: India's Hopes Ride on Yuki Bhambri and the Doubles Brigade
excerpt: With no Indian in the singles draw, a top-20 Bhambri leads a seasoned doubles contingent onto the SW19 grass when the Championships begin Monday.
body:
British summer means strawberries, cream and, for India's tennis followers, a familiar question: who carries the tricolour onto the lawns of SW19? As the 2026 Wimbledon Championships approach, set to begin on Monday, 29 June, the answer once again lies not in the singles draw but in doubles, where a small but seasoned Indian contingent arrives in the best collective form the country has had on grass in years.

## Bhambri leads the charge

The standout is **Yuki Bhambri**. The 33-year-old from New Delhi, a former junior world No. 1 who won the Australian Open boys' title back in 2009, has reinvented himself as one of the most reliable doubles players on the ATP Tour. In February 2026 he climbed to a career-high doubles ranking of world No. 18 — comfortably the highest of any Indian man — and he comes to Wimbledon riding the momentum of a breakthrough 2025 season.

That season included a run to the **US Open semifinals**, a third round at Wimbledon, and a third round at Roland Garros, results that turned a player once defined by chronic injuries into a fixture in the latter stages of majors. Bhambri, who is based in Bradenton, Florida, has long been a transatlantic figure, and grass — where his flat hitting and quick hands reward aggression at the net — suits his game.

## A deeper Indian bench

Bhambri is not alone. India's doubles depth now stretches across the tour. **N. Sriram Balaji**, the Davis Cup mainstay, and **Rithvik Bollipalli** have both been building ranking points on the ATP circuit, while veterans of the doubles game continue to give India a presence in the men's draw that its singles ranks can no longer match. On the women's side, the absence of a singles entrant is offset by the steady international schedule India's doubles specialists keep.

The singles picture is the sobering counterpoint. **Sumit Nagal**, long India's No. 1, has slipped outside the rankings band needed for direct entry or qualifying at the majors, leaving India without a man or woman in the singles main draw at Wimbledon for another year. It is a gap that underscores how completely India's modern tennis identity has become a doubles story — a lineage that runs from Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi through Rohan Bopanna and Sania Mirza to the players teeing off this fortnight.

## What's at stake

Wimbledon 2026 is also a landmark edition. The All England Club has, for the first time in the tournament's history, introduced electronic video review for line calls on its show courts, and the total prize pot has risen to a record £64.2 million — a 20 percent jump on 2025, with even first-round losers collecting meaningful cheques. For doubles players who grind out a living across continents, the richer purse matters: a deep run can fund months of travel and coaching.

For Bhambri specifically, a strong showing would tighten his grip on a top-20 ranking and strengthen his case for the season-ending ATP Finals in doubles, a stage no Indian has reached in some time. The draw, released this week, will determine the opening assignments, with first-round matches beginning Monday.

## The diaspora angle

For the millions of Indians and people of Indian origin living in Britain, the United States, Canada and Australia, Wimbledon is the most accessible major on the calendar — played in English, broadcast in friendly time zones for the UK and East Coast, and steeped in the kind of tradition the diaspora grew up watching on television back home. Seeing an Indian name on the order of play at the world's most famous tennis tournament remains a point of quiet pride, and in 2026 that name is most likely to be Bhambri's. For NRIs, the success of Indian athletes like Bhambri on the global stage also reinforces a sense of connection to their heritage and can inspire younger generations within the diaspora to pursue their own athletic dreams.

India's grass-court ambitions may be narrower than they once were, but they are far from extinguished. As the white kit comes out and the covers come off, the country's doubles specialists will again carry the hopes of a fan base scattered across the globe — proof that even without a singles star, India still has a seat at tennis's grandest table.
